title: Creation, Eden and the Akedah
bigQuestion: What does a reader find in Genesis when the text is read slowly, word by word, with its oldest and newest readers at the table?

story.title: Counting the Words Isaac Never Says
story.kicker: Two students take a highlighter to Genesis 22 and go looking for what Isaac was thinking.
paragraphs: Maya and Devin have a copy of Genesis 22 on the table, nineteen verses in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation. The assignment is simple. Highlight every word that tells you what Isaac feels or thinks. They expect to be busy. A father takes his son up a mountain to offer him as a sacrifice. Surely the text says something about the boy.

Devin reads out loud. Abraham gets up early. Abraham saddles the donkey. Abraham cuts the wood. Abraham lifts up his eyes and sees the place. Maya's highlighter stays capped. Then Isaac speaks, once. "My father," he says, and asks where the lamb is. Abraham answers that God will see to the lamb. Then the text says they went on, both of them together.

Maya counts again. Isaac says twenty or so words in the whole chapter. The text never says he is afraid. It never says he is confused, or brave, or that he trusts his father. It does not say how old he is. It does not say what he does when he is untied. At the end of the story, Abraham goes back down to his servants. The verse does not mention Isaac at all.

Devin is frustrated. "The writer left out everything I want to know." Their teacher smiles, because that is the point of the lesson. Nearly three thousand years of readers have noticed the same silence. The rabbis of the midrash wrote conversations to fill it. Medieval commentators argued about Isaac's age. A German scholar in 1946 said this silence is what makes the Bible's style what it is.

This chapter reads three passages of Genesis this way: the seven days of creation, the garden of Eden, and the binding of Isaac. Each one is short. Each one has been read for a very long time by Jewish readers, by Christian readers, by historians and by people who simply love a good story. The goal is to see what the words say, what they leave out, and what different readers have done with the gaps.
story.think: Why might a writer leave out what a character is feeling? What does the reader have to do when the text stays silent?

lessons.title: A Pattern Built From Refrains
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 1:1–2:3 is built on a strict pattern of repeated phrases, and the pattern itself is part of the meaning.
reading: The Tanakh opens with *Bereshit*, the Hebrew word that gives the book of Genesis its Hebrew name. The first account of creation runs from Genesis 1:1 to 2:3. Read it slowly and the same phrases keep returning. "And God said." "And it was so." "And God saw that it was good." "And there was evening and there was morning." Each day closes with that last line, like a bell at the end of a class period. These repeated lines are called *refrains*, and they give the passage the feel of a poem or a liturgy more than a report.

Readers have long noticed a shape inside the seven days. Days one to three create spaces: light and dark, sky and sea, dry land and plants. Days four to six fill those spaces: sun, moon and stars for the light; birds and fish for sky and sea; animals and humans for the land. Day three and day six each have two acts of creation. The seventh day is different. Nothing is made. God rests, and the day is blessed and made holy. Jewish tradition reads this as the root of *Shabbat*, the weekly day of rest.

The name for God in this passage is Elohim, translated "God." It is used the same way from the first verse to the last. Creation happens through speech. God speaks, and the thing exists. There is no fight and no rival. Humans are made last, male and female together, and are said to be made in the image of God. The text does not explain what that image means. Rabbinic and later readers have offered many answers, and this course will meet several of them. What the passage itself gives is order, rhythm and a world declared good.

words.d: "In the beginning," the first Hebrew word of the Torah and the Hebrew name for the book of Genesis
a line or phrase repeated at regular points in a text, such as "and there was evening and there was morning"
the Jewish day of rest, from Friday evening to Saturday evening, which Jewish tradition roots in the seventh day of creation

look.title: The First Verse
look.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
look.prompt: Ten words in English, seven in Hebrew. What does this verse say, and what does it leave unsaid about how, why, or when?

check.q: Which phrase closes each of the six days of creation in Genesis 1?
choices: And there was evening and there was morning
And God rested from all His work
And the LORD God planted a garden
check.why: The evening-and-morning line is the refrain that ends each day in Genesis 1; the other phrases come from day seven, Genesis 2 or the opening verse.

check.q: How do days four to six relate to days one to three?
choices: They undo the first three days
They fill the spaces the first three days created
They repeat the first three days word for word
check.why: Readers have long noticed that days one to three make spaces (light, sky and sea, land) and days four to six fill them (lights, birds and fish, animals and humans).

check.q: What name for God is used throughout Genesis 1:1–2:3?
check.why: The first creation account uses Elohim, "God," all the way through; "the LORD God" appears in the second account starting at Genesis 2:4.

lessons.title: Three Commentators on Verse One
lessons.mainIdea: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Ramban each read the first verse differently, and their disagreement is part of how Jewish tradition studies Torah.
reading: Jewish study of the Torah has always happened with commentators on the page. The three most read medieval commentators are *Rashi* (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, France, 1040–1105), Abraham *Ibn Ezra* (Spain, c. 1089–1164) and *Ramban* (Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman, Spain, 1194–1270). In a traditional printed Bible their words surround the text. On Genesis 1:1 they do not agree, and generations of students have learned to read by watching them argue.

Rashi opens with a question he takes from an earlier rabbi. The Torah is a book of commandments, so why does it not begin with the first commandment given to Israel, in Exodus 12? Rashi answers that the Torah begins with creation so that Israel can say the whole earth belongs to God, who gives land to whom God chooses. Then Rashi turns to grammar. He reads the Hebrew bereshit as "in the beginning of," so the verse means "when God began to create," and he says the verse does not teach the order in which things were made.

Ibn Ezra, a grammarian, also reads bereshit as a phrase that leans on the next words, and he warns against reading too much into a single verse. Ramban pushes back. He argues that the verb bara, "created," is used only for making something from nothing, and that verse one teaches exactly that: God brought the raw material of the world into being from nothing at all. Ramban also says the deep meaning of creation cannot be learned from the verses alone. Three readers, one verse, three results. That is what close reading with the commentators looks like.

words.d: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105), the most widely studied Jewish commentator on the Torah and Talmud
Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1164), a Spanish Jewish commentator known for close attention to Hebrew grammar
Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman, or Nachmanides (1194–1270), a Spanish commentator who often argues with Rashi
a written explanation of a text, verse by verse, printed beside the text it explains

look.title: Two Ways to Start a Sentence
look.text: The 1917 JPS translation begins: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The 1985 JPS translation, following Rashi's grammar, begins instead with a "When" clause, so that God's first act of creating is described as the earth was still unformed and dark. In the first reading, verse one is a complete statement. In the second, verse one is only the start of a longer sentence that reaches its main action at "Let there be light."
look.prompt: What changes about the story if verse one is a complete sentence, and what changes if it is only the opening clause? Which reading does Ramban need?

check.q: Why, according to the question Rashi opens with, might the Torah have started at Exodus 12 instead of Genesis 1?
choices: Because Exodus 12 is written in Aramaic
Because Exodus is older than Genesis
Because Moses is born in Exodus
Because Exodus 12 holds the first commandment given to Israel
check.why: Rashi asks why a book of commandments does not begin with the first commandment, which comes in Exodus 12, and answers that creation shows the earth belongs to God.

check.q: Which commentator argues that the verb "created" means making something from nothing?
check.why: Ramban holds that bara is used only for creation from nothing and that Genesis 1:1 teaches this; Rashi and Ibn Ezra focus on the grammar of bereshit.

check.q: What do Rashi and Ibn Ezra share in reading the first word, bereshit?
choices: They both say it names a place
They both read it as "in the beginning of," leaning on the next words
They both say it means "on the seventh day"
They both read it as a name of God
check.why: Both read bereshit as a construct phrase, so the verse means roughly "when God began to create"; this is why the 1985 JPS translation starts with "When."

lessons.title: Enuma Elish Beside Genesis 1
lessons.mainIdea: Reading Genesis 1 next to the Babylonian creation epic shows what the two texts share and where Genesis makes different choices.
reading: In the 1840s and 1850s, British excavators at Nineveh, in what is now northern Iraq, uncovered thousands of clay tablets from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. Among them were pieces of a Babylonian poem now called *Enuma Elish*, after its first words, "When on high." George Smith of the British Museum published an English account of it in 1876. For the first time, readers of Genesis could set the biblical creation story beside an older neighbor written in *cuneiform*, the wedge-shaped script of Mesopotamia.

Enuma Elish tells of a fight among gods. The young god Marduk kills the sea goddess Tiamat, splits her body, and makes the sky from one half and the earth from the other. Humans are made from the blood of a defeated god so that the gods can rest from labor. The poem ends with Marduk's temple in Babylon and his fifty names. Scholars note some points of contact with Genesis 1: water and darkness at the start, a sky that holds back waters above, a sequence that ends in rest. Many also point out that the Hebrew word for the deep, tehom, sounds like the name Tiamat.

The differences are just as clear, and readers have drawn different lessons from them. In Genesis 1 there is one God, no battle and no rival. Creation happens by speech. The sun and moon, gods in Babylon, are called simply the greater and lesser lights. Humans are not slaves of the gods but are made in God's image and told to rule over the earth. Some historians read Genesis 1 as a quiet argument with the Babylonian story, perhaps written or shaped during the Babylonian exile in the 500s BCE. Traditional Jewish readers, who hold the Torah to be given by God, generally see the contrast as the Torah's teaching against the beliefs of Israel's neighbors. Both readings start from the same comparison.

words.d: the Babylonian creation poem, named for its opening words "When on high"; found on tablets from Nineveh
the wedge-shaped writing system of ancient Mesopotamia, pressed into clay tablets
the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, home of Babylon and Assyria; now mostly Iraq

look.title: Two Beginnings Side by Side
look.text: Enuma Elish (in summary): before sky and earth had names, fresh and salt waters mingled. Gods were born. War broke out. Marduk slew Tiamat, split her like a shellfish, and set half of her as the sky to hold back her waters. Genesis 1 (in summary): the earth was unformed, darkness was over the deep, and God said, "Let there be light." On the second day God made a firmament to divide the waters below from the waters above.
look.prompt: List one thing the two accounts share and two things Genesis does differently. What might each difference be saying?

check.q: Where were the tablets of Enuma Elish found?
choices: In a cave near the Dead Sea
In the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh
In a synagogue storeroom in Cairo
check.why: Excavators at Nineveh in the mid-1800s recovered Ashurbanipal's library, which held the Babylonian creation poem; the other sites yielded different famous finds.

check.q: In Enuma Elish, how are the sky and earth made?
choices: By a word spoken in the dark
By the potter god shaping clay
From the split body of the defeated goddess Tiamat
check.why: The poem says Marduk splits Tiamat and forms sky and earth from her halves; Genesis 1, by contrast, has creation by speech and no battle.

check.q: Why do some scholars connect the Hebrew word tehom with the Babylonian story?
choices: It sounds like the name Tiamat
It is the name of Marduk's temple
check.why: Tehom, "the deep" in Genesis 1:2, sounds like Tiamat, the sea goddess; scholars treat the likeness as one possible point of contact between the texts.

lessons.title: A Second Way to Begin
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 2:4–3:24 tells creation again, with a different order, a different name for God and a different style.
reading: At Genesis 2:4 the text starts over. "These are the generations of the heaven and of the earth," it says, and then tells a story that does not match the first account point for point. In Genesis 1 plants come on day three, animals on days five and six, and humans last. In Genesis 2 there is no rain and no plant yet when God forms the man from the dust of the ground. Then God plants a garden in *Eden*, then forms the animals, and only then makes the woman from the man's side. Close readers have noticed this for a very long time.

The name for God changes, too. Genesis 1 says Elohim, "God." From Genesis 2:4 the text says "the LORD God," pairing the four-letter name of God, which Jewish practice does not pronounce, with Elohim. The style changes as well. Genesis 1 is a list with refrains and no dialogue. Genesis 2 and 3 are a story with a garden, two named rivers among four, a talking serpent, questions and answers. God is described walking in the garden in the cool of the day. The first account looks up at the sky; the second kneels in the dirt.

Jewish readers across the centuries have handled the two accounts in more than one way. Rashi, following the rabbis, treats Genesis 2 as adding detail to Genesis 1 and reads the differences as answers to questions the first chapter leaves open. The Talmud in tractate Berakhot notes the two names of God and links them to two ways God relates to the world, justice and mercy. Modern academic scholars, whom the next lessons will meet, read the two accounts as coming from different sources. What every reader shares is the observation itself: the Torah gives creation twice, and the second telling is not the first.

words.d: the garden in Genesis 2–3 where the first humans are placed; the name is used in Hebrew for delight
the way JPS 1917 renders the four-letter personal name of God, which Jewish practice does not pronounce
the JPS 1917 rendering of toledot, a Hebrew heading in Genesis that introduces a new account or family line

look.title: Two Orders of Creation
look.text: Genesis 1, in order: light; sky; land and plants; sun, moon and stars; fish and birds; land animals, then humans, male and female together. Genesis 2, in order: the man from dust; a garden with trees; the animals, brought to the man to be named; the woman, built from the man's side. In Genesis 1, God is called God. In Genesis 2, God is called the LORD God.
look.prompt: Name two differences in order between the accounts. Then suggest one way Rashi might read them as one story and one way a modern scholar might read them as two.

check.q: Which comes first in Genesis 2, according to the order of the text?
check.why: Genesis 2 forms the man first, then plants the garden, then forms the animals, and last builds the woman; the sun and moon belong to the Genesis 1 sequence.

check.q: How does the name for God change at Genesis 2:4?
check.why: Genesis 1 uses Elohim; from 2:4 the text pairs the four-letter name, written "the LORD" in JPS 1917, with Elohim.

check.q: How does Rashi, following the rabbis, handle the two creation accounts?
choices: He says the second account is a later addition by a scribe
He says Genesis 1 should be ignored
He says the two accounts describe two different worlds
He reads Genesis 2 as adding detail to Genesis 1
check.why: Rashi treats Genesis 2 as filling in the first chapter, answering questions it leaves open; the source-based reading belongs to modern academic scholarship.

lessons.title: The Serpent and the Question
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 3 turns on wordplay, dialogue and a question from God, and each of these has been read closely by Jewish readers.
reading: Genesis 2 ends with the man and woman naked and unashamed. Genesis 3 begins with the *serpent*, called the most "subtle" of the animals. In Hebrew the two verses sit side by side on a pun. The humans are arummim, naked; the serpent is arum, cunning. The sound is nearly the same. Readers who know Hebrew have long heard the link, and translators struggle to carry it into English. The pun tells the reader that the story of the garden is going to be about knowing and not knowing.

The serpent's first words are a question about what God said. The woman answers, adding a rule the text did not record: not even to touch the tree. The serpent promises that eating will open their eyes and make them like God, knowing good and evil. They eat. Their eyes open, and what they know first is that they are naked. They sew fig leaves and hide. The text moves quickly, through short lines of dialogue, and never explains what the *knowledge of good and evil* is. Readers have proposed moral judgment, adult awareness, or simply all knowledge; the text does not settle it.

Then comes one of the most discussed questions in the Torah. God calls to the man, "Where art thou?" Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says God of course knew where the man was. God opened with a question so as not to frighten him, giving him room to answer. The man's answer shifts blame to the woman, and the woman's to the serpent. The chapter ends with the consequences for each: the serpent on its belly, pain in childbirth, hard work for the ground, and the two sent out of Eden, with *cherubim* and a turning sword at the gate. The text does not use the word sin, and it does not use the word fall.

words.d: the talking snake of Genesis 3, called the most subtle of the animals; the text does not identify it further
what the forbidden tree gives in Genesis 2–3; readers disagree about what kind of knowing it means
winged beings placed at the east of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life; the plural of cherub

look.title: The First Question
look.text: And the LORD God called unto the man, and said unto him: 'Where art thou?'
look.prompt: Rashi says God asked so the man would not be afraid. What else could a question do that a statement could not? What does the man do with the opening he is given?

check.q: What pun links the end of Genesis 2 with the start of Genesis 3?
choices: The Hebrew words for naked and cunning sound alike
The words for tree and life are the same
Eden and Adam are spelled the same
check.why: Arummim (naked, 2:25) and arum (subtle or cunning, 3:1) sit side by side; readers of the Hebrew hear the play on sound.

check.q: How does Rashi explain why God asks the man where he is?
choices: God had lost track of the man in the garden
God opened with a question so as not to frighten him and to give him room to answer
The question was really addressed to the serpent
The verse is a later scribe's addition
check.why: Rashi, following the midrash, says God knew and asked in order to open a conversation gently; the other choices are not readings found in Rashi.

check.q: Which words does Genesis 3 not use, even though later readers often attach them to the chapter?
check.why: Genesis 3 never says sin or fall; those terms come from later readers, and the next lesson shows how Jewish and Christian traditions differ on them.

lessons.title: Eden in the Midrash and Beyond
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish and Christian traditions read the garden story differently, and midrash fills its gaps in its own way.
reading: *Midrash* is the rabbinic way of reading that asks what a text leaves out and answers with story, law or teaching. The largest collection on Genesis is *Genesis Rabbah*, compiled in the land of Israel around the 400s CE. On Eden it asks many questions. From what earth was the first human formed? One answer: from dust gathered from the whole world, so that no land could claim him. Why was the woman built from the side and not the head or the foot? One answer: so that she would be neither above nor beneath the man. These are readings, offered by named rabbis, and often several are placed side by side without choosing.

The midrash also reads the garden as a story about consequences rather than an inherited condition. In rabbinic thought, each person is born with two inclinations, the yetzer ha-tov and the yetzer ha-ra, a pull toward good and a pull toward selfishness, and each person chooses. The garden explains why humans die and work hard and why the world is not Eden. It does not, in the mainstream Jewish reading, make later humans guilty for what the first two did. The word Adam is also simply the Hebrew for human, and the rabbis play on that.

Christian tradition took a different road. The apostle Paul, in his letter to the Romans, read Adam as the one through whom sin and death entered the world. Augustine of Hippo, writing around 400 CE, developed this into the doctrine of *original sin*, the teaching that all humans inherit a fallen state from Adam. Many Christian traditions hold this; some Christian readers read it differently. Jewish tradition as a whole did not adopt it. The same three chapters, read by two communities, became two different stories about what it means to be human. A careful reader can describe both without deciding between them.

words.d: rabbinic interpretation that fills the gaps in a biblical text with story, law or teaching; also a collection of such readings
the major rabbinic midrash on Genesis, compiled in the land of Israel around the 400s CE
the Christian doctrine, developed by Augustine, that humans inherit a fallen state from Adam; not a Jewish teaching
in rabbinic thought, the inclination toward selfish desire, paired with the yetzer ha-tov, the inclination toward good

look.title: One Garden, Two Readings
look.text: Rabbinic reading (in summary): the story of Eden explains death, hard work and exile from the garden. Every person still chooses between two inclinations, and the text says nothing about inherited guilt. Augustine's reading (in summary): Adam's act changed human nature itself, so every person is born in a fallen state and needs God's grace to be healed. Both readers are looking at the same verses in Genesis 3.
look.prompt: Find one detail in Genesis 3 each reader might point to. How would you describe the difference between the two readings without saying which is right?

check.q: What is Genesis Rabbah?
choices: A rabbinic midrash collection on Genesis, compiled around the 400s CE
check.why: Genesis Rabbah is the major midrash on Genesis; Rashi's commentary, Enuma Elish and the Septuagint are different works.

check.q: Which idea belongs to Augustine's reading of Genesis 3 but not to the mainstream rabbinic reading?
choices: Humans inherit a fallen state from Adam
The garden story explains why humans die
God asked the man a question
check.why: Original sin, the inherited fallen state, is Augustine's doctrine; Jewish tradition reads the story as explaining death and exile while each person still chooses.

check.q: In rabbinic thought, what are the yetzer ha-tov and the yetzer ha-ra?
choices: Two inclinations in each person, toward good and toward selfish desire
check.why: The rabbis describe every person as having a pull toward good and a pull toward selfishness; the two trees and the rivers are features of the garden itself.

lessons.title: The Documentary Hypothesis in Brief
lessons.mainIdea: Modern academic scholars explain the doubled stories of the Torah as woven from several sources, and Jewish readers have responded in several ways.
reading: By the 1800s, scholars in European universities had gathered the puzzles that close readers had always seen: two creation accounts, two names for God, two versions of some stories, laws that repeat with changes. The German scholar Julius Wellhausen, in a book published in 1878, gave these puzzles a full theory. The Torah, he argued, was woven together from four written *sources*, later called J, E, D and P for the clues that mark them. J uses the four-letter name of God from the start; E prefers Elohim; D is most of Deuteronomy; P is the priestly material, with its lists, dates and laws of worship. This is the *documentary hypothesis*.

On the theory, Genesis 1:1–2:3, with its refrains and its Elohim, is P. Genesis 2:4–3:24, with the LORD God, the garden and the dialogue, is J. Scholars who hold the theory have argued for more than a century about dates, about whether E ever existed on its own and about how the sources were joined. Today many academic scholars keep the basic idea of several sources while rejecting Wellhausen's details. Others prefer models of layers added over time. It remains a hypothesis, a proposed explanation, and it is taught as such in universities, including in Israel.

Jewish responses have ranged widely. Wellhausen's own writing carried a low view of later Judaism, and in 1903 Solomon Schechter, a leading Jewish scholar in New York, called this kind of criticism "higher anti-Semitism." The Italian-Israeli scholar Umberto Cassuto argued in lectures in the 1940s that the Torah was a single work and the sources a mirage. Orthodox Judaism holds that the Torah was given to Moses by God and does not accept the hypothesis as an account of how the Torah came to be. Conservative and Reform Judaism generally teach it in their seminaries alongside traditional study. Some scholars, such as Richard Elliott Friedman, are both observant Jews and source critics. A student in a public school describes these positions; the class does not vote on them.

words.d: the academic theory that the Torah was woven from several written sources, often labeled J, E, D and P
in biblical scholarship, an earlier written document that a later editor is thought to have used
Julius Wellhausen (1844–1918), the German scholar whose 1878 book gave the documentary hypothesis its classic form
a proposed explanation that is tested against evidence; it may be widely held and still be open to revision

look.title: Genesis by the Numbers
look.cite: Standard chapter and verse divisions; the annual parashah cycle
look.prompt: Genesis has 12 weekly portions and 50 chapters. Which of these divisions is older, the chapters or the portions? What would you need to know to answer?

check.q: Under the documentary hypothesis, what marks the source called P?
choices: The four-letter name of God from the start
Priestly material such as lists, dates and laws of worship
Stories set in the northern kingdom
check.why: P is the priestly source, credited with Genesis 1, genealogies and worship law; J is marked by the divine name, D by Deuteronomy.

check.q: What did Solomon Schechter call the biblical criticism of his day in a 1903 address?
check.why: Schechter's address titled the movement "Higher Criticism, Higher Anti-Semitism," objecting to the low view of Judaism in some of its leading writers.

check.q: Which statement correctly describes the range of Jewish responses to the hypothesis?
choices: Only Reform Judaism has ever discussed it
Responses range from rejection to teaching it alongside traditional study
check.why: Orthodox Judaism does not accept it as an account of the Torah's origin, Cassuto argued against it, and Conservative and Reform seminaries teach it; some observant scholars practice source criticism.

lessons.title: Reading the Journey Word by Word
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 22 is told in spare, exact words, and its repetitions carry the weight of the story.
reading: Jewish tradition calls Genesis 22 the *Akedah*, the Binding, from the verb used when Abraham binds Isaac. The chapter opens by telling the reader something Abraham does not know: God is testing him. Then God calls, and Abraham answers with one Hebrew word, *hineni*, "here am I." He will say it three times in the chapter, once to God, once to Isaac, once to the angel. The command is built up in steps: your son, your only son, whom you love, Isaac. Rashi, following the Talmud, reads it as a conversation, with Abraham answering each phrase, "I have two sons," "each is the only son of his mother," "I love them both," until the name closes every door.

The text says nothing about the night that follows. Abraham rises early, saddles the donkey, takes two servants and Isaac, cuts the wood and goes. Three days pass in a single verse. On the third day Abraham lifts his eyes and sees the place from afar. He tells the servants to wait, and says that he and the lad will worship and return. Abraham puts the wood on Isaac. He carries the fire and the knife himself. Then comes a line the chapter will repeat: "and they went both of them together."

Isaac speaks once. "My father." Abraham answers, "Here am I, my son." Isaac observes that they have fire and wood, and asks where the lamb is. Abraham answers that God will see to the lamb, and adds, "my son." Then the line returns: "and they went both of them together." Read slowly, the second time is not the first. Before the question, they walk together in silence. After the question, they walk together knowing more, or perhaps the same. The text does not say. What it gives is the repetition, and the reader has to decide what changed between the two.

words.d: "the Binding," the Jewish name for Genesis 22, where Abraham binds Isaac on the altar
"here am I," the Hebrew word of readiness Abraham speaks three times in Genesis 22
the land where Genesis 22 is set; 2 Chronicles 3:1 uses the name for the Temple mount in Jerusalem

look.title: The Command in Steps
look.text: And He said: 'Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt-offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.'
look.prompt: Count the steps before the name Isaac is spoken. Why might the text delay the name? What does Rashi do with the delay?

check.q: What does hineni mean, and who says it in Genesis 22?
choices: "Do not lay your hand"; the angel, once
check.why: Hineni, "here am I," is Abraham's answer to God, to Isaac and to the angel; Isaac's question and the angel's command are different lines.

check.q: Which line does Genesis 22 repeat, before and after Isaac's question?
choices: "And they went both of them together"
check.why: The phrase about walking together appears in verse 6 and again in verse 8, framing the only exchange between father and son.

check.q: How does Rashi read the four-step command "thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac"?
choices: As four different sons of Abraham
As a list of four mountains
As a conversation in which Abraham answers each phrase
As proof that Isaac was an adult
check.why: Rashi, drawing on the Talmud, imagines Abraham replying to each phrase until the name Isaac leaves no other possibility.

lessons.title: The Gaps and the Silence
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 22 leaves out what its characters feel, and this silence shapes how the story has been read for centuries.
reading: Two students with a highlighter find what scholars have found. Genesis 22 never says what Isaac thinks. It does not give his age. It does not say whether he struggles when bound or what he does when released. Sarah, his mother, is not mentioned in the chapter at all. When it ends, the text says Abraham returned to his young men, and they went together to Beer-sheba. Isaac's name is absent from that verse. The reader who wants to know what happened to him must look elsewhere or imagine.

The German scholar Erich *Auerbach*, writing in exile in Istanbul during the Second World War, opened his book Mimesis (1946) by setting this chapter beside a scene from Homer's Odyssey. Homer, he argued, lights everything: every object, every feeling, every past event is described in the foreground. Genesis does the opposite. It gives only what is needed, and everything else stays in the background, unspoken. Auerbach said this makes the biblical text "fraught with background" and demanding. It calls the reader into the story to supply what is missing.

Jewish readers had been answering that call for centuries. Genesis Rabbah gives Isaac words: he asks his father to bind him tightly so he will not flinch. Rashi on the next chapter connects Sarah's death, reported in Genesis 23:2, to the news of what nearly happened on the mountain. The rabbis debated whether Isaac was a child or a grown man of thirty-seven, because Sarah's age gives room for either answer. These fillings are not the text. They are *midrash*, and the tradition keeps them clearly marked as such, printed beside the verses rather than inside them.

words.d: Erich Auerbach (1892–1957), whose book Mimesis (1946) compared the spare style of Genesis 22 with Homer
something a narrative leaves out, such as a character's thoughts, which the reader or a later interpreter may fill
the town in the south of the land where Abraham lived and to which he returns after Genesis 22

look.title: What the Chapter Does Not Say
look.text: Read Genesis 22:1–19 in JPS 1917 and make three lists. First: every action Abraham takes. Second: every word Isaac speaks. Third: every word that names a feeling, a thought or a motive of either one. Most readers find the first list long, the second list very short and the third list nearly empty. Now read Genesis 23:1–2, where Sarah's death is reported without a stated cause.
look.prompt: What would you have to add to the story to know how Isaac felt? Where does Rashi find a place to add something about Sarah?

check.q: Who is absent from the final verse of the Akedah story, Genesis 22:19?
check.why: Verse 19 says Abraham returned to his young men and went to Beer-sheba; Isaac is not named, which readers have long noticed.

check.q: What contrast did Auerbach draw in the opening chapter of Mimesis?
choices: Between the Torah and the Talmud
Between the foregrounded style of Homer and the background-filled style of Genesis
check.why: Auerbach set the scar scene from the Odyssey beside Genesis 22 to show Homer lighting everything and the Bible leaving nearly everything unspoken.

check.q: How does Jewish tradition treat midrashic fillings such as Isaac asking to be bound tightly?
choices: As readings printed beside the text, not as the text itself
As verses added to the Torah scroll
As proof that the story is not in Genesis
As part of the JPS 1917 translation
check.why: Midrash is interpretation kept distinct from the verses; it appears in collections like Genesis Rabbah and in commentary, never inside the Torah text.

lessons.title: The Ram, the Age and the Test
lessons.mainIdea: The end of the Akedah and the age of Isaac are read differently by midrash, Ibn Ezra and Ramban, showing how commentators weigh a text.
reading: At the climax, an angel calls from heaven and Abraham answers, hineni, for the third time. He is told not to lay a hand on the boy, for now it is known that he fears God. Abraham lifts his eyes and sees a *ram* caught by its horns in a thicket, and offers it in place of his son. He names the place with a phrase built on the verb to see. The angel speaks again, promising blessing and many descendants. In the whole chapter, the ram is the one unexpected thing, and the rabbis gave it a history: some versions of a list in Pirkei Avot count the ram of Abraham among things made at the twilight of the sixth day of creation.

How old was Isaac? The text calls him a na'ar, a lad, a word used for both boys and young men. Genesis Rabbah reasons from Sarah's death at 127 in the next chapter, which it connects to the Akedah, and concludes Isaac was 37. Ibn Ezra rejects this. If Isaac had been a grown man, he writes, the text would have recorded his obedience as a merit of his own, and it does not. Ibn Ezra estimates Isaac was near 13. This is a good example of two readers using the same verses and different rules of evidence. The midrash reads across chapters and fills gaps; Ibn Ezra reads the plain sense and asks what the text would have said.

What kind of test is it? Ramban asks the question that many students ask: God, who knows everything, does not need to learn anything from a test. Ramban answers that the test is for the one tested, to turn a good intention into a completed act, so that Abraham's willingness becomes a deed and earns its reward. Other readers ask whether the test was whether Abraham would obey, or whether he would refuse. The text says only that the test happened and that Abraham passed, in the words of the angel. Every reading after that is a reading, and a careful student says whose it is.

words.d: the male sheep caught in the thicket in Genesis 22:13, offered in place of Isaac
the Hebrew word for a lad or young man used of Isaac in Genesis 22; it does not fix his age
the plain sense of a text, read in its context and grammar; the method Ibn Ezra favors

look.title: How Old Was Isaac?
look.text: Genesis Rabbah (in summary): Sarah dies at 127 at the start of Genesis 23. Isaac was born when she was 90. If her death followed the news of the Akedah, Isaac was 37 when bound. Ibn Ezra on Genesis 22:4 (in summary): if Isaac had been a grown man, his willingness would have been a merit the text would record. It records only Abraham's. So Isaac was a boy, close to 13, old enough to carry wood and ask a question.
look.prompt: Each reader uses evidence. Name the evidence each one uses and the rule of reading behind it. Which kind of evidence do you find stronger, and why?

check.q: What does Ibn Ezra conclude about Isaac's age, and from what?
choices: About 37, from Sarah's age at death
Near 13, because the text records no merit of Isaac's own
Exactly 40, from the age at his marriage
An infant, because he is carried
check.why: Ibn Ezra reasons that a grown man's willingness would have been recorded as his own merit; since only Abraham's is, Isaac was a boy near 13.

check.q: How does Ramban answer the question of why an all-knowing God would test Abraham?
choices: The test is for God to learn what Abraham will do
The test is a later addition
The test is for the one tested, so that a good intention becomes a deed
The test proves that Isaac was an adult
check.why: Ramban says the test benefits the person tested by turning willingness into a completed act; the other answers are not his reading.

check.q: Which word in Genesis 22 describes Isaac but does not fix his age?
check.why: Na'ar means a lad or young man and is used for people of a range of ages, which is why the commentators can disagree.

lessons.title: The Akedah in the Year and in Modern Thought
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 22 is read aloud every Rosh Hashanah and has been argued over by modern thinkers of several traditions.
reading: On the second day of *Rosh Hashanah*, the Jewish new year, the Torah reading in the synagogue is Genesis 22. The Talmud, in tractate Megillah, sets this reading. The holiday's central sound is the *shofar*, usually a ram's horn. In tractate Rosh Hashanah, Rabbi Abbahu asks why a ram's horn is used, and answers in God's voice: sound a ram's horn before me so that I remember for you the binding of Isaac son of Abraham. The Zichronot, the remembrance prayers of the holiday's additional service, ask God to recall the Akedah and treat the people with mercy for its sake. In Jewish practice, the chapter is not only a story about Abraham; it is an appeal.

Modern thinkers have pulled the chapter in other directions. The Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard, in Fear and Trembling (1843), made Abraham the model of faith precisely because his obedience cannot be explained by ethics. Kierkegaard called this a suspension of the ethical, and he wrote as a Christian for a Christian audience. The Israeli thinker Yeshayahu Leibowitz, in the twentieth century, read the Akedah as the purest picture of Jewish worship: serving God for God's sake, not for human need. The British poet Wilfred Owen, writing from the trenches of the First World War, retold the story with the old man refusing the ram and killing his son, and half the sons of Europe with him.

After the Holocaust, the chapter grew heavier still. Israeli poets and painters returned to Isaac as the one who was bound and did not speak. Some Jewish thinkers asked whether the point of the story is the command or the angel's voice that stops the knife. A public school class cannot settle these questions and should not try. It can read the nineteen verses carefully, name the readers and their traditions, and notice how a text this short has carried so much. That is the method of this whole unit: text first, then readers, then the student's own reasoned response.

words.d: the Jewish new year, in early autumn; Genesis 22 is the Torah reading on its second day
a horn, usually a ram's, sounded on Rosh Hashanah; the Talmud links it to the ram of the Akedah
Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855), Danish Christian philosopher whose Fear and Trembling (1843) is a famous reading of the Akedah

look.title: Why a Ram's Horn?
look.text: Rabbi Abbahu asked why the shofar is sounded with a ram's horn. He answered that the Holy One says: sound a ram's horn before me, so that I will remember for you the binding of Isaac son of Abraham, and count it for you as if you had bound yourselves before me.
look.prompt: In this reading, who is the Akedah for, and what is the community asking for when the shofar sounds?

check.q: When is Genesis 22 read aloud in the synagogue each year?
choices: On the second day of Rosh Hashanah
On the first night of Passover
check.why: The Talmud in tractate Megillah assigns the Akedah to the second day of Rosh Hashanah; the other holidays have their own readings.

check.q: How does Rabbi Abbahu in the Talmud connect the shofar to Genesis 22?
choices: The shofar was found in the thicket
A ram's horn is sounded so God will remember the binding of Isaac
Abraham blew a shofar on the mountain
check.why: Rosh Hashanah 16a has God ask for a ram's horn so that the Akedah is remembered on the people's behalf.

check.q: Which description of Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling is accurate?
choices: A rabbinic midrash from the 400s CE
A Talmudic passage on the shofar
A Christian philosopher's 1843 reading of Abraham as a model of faith beyond ethics
A poem from the First World War
check.why: Kierkegaard, a Danish Christian philosopher, published Fear and Trembling in 1843; Owen wrote the wartime poem, and the midrash and Talmud are much older.

review.q: Which of these is a difference between Genesis 1 and Genesis 2–3?
choices: Genesis 2 uses refrains for each day
Genesis 1 uses "God" while Genesis 2–3 uses "the LORD God"
review.why: The change in the divine name at Genesis 2:4 is one of the clearest differences between the two accounts.

review.q: Which commentator reads Genesis 1:1 as teaching creation from nothing?
review.why: Ramban insists the verb bara means making from nothing; Rashi and Ibn Ezra focus on grammar, and Wellhausen was a modern source critic.

review.q: What did George Smith publish in 1876?
choices: The first JPS translation of Genesis
An English account of the Babylonian creation poem from Nineveh
review.why: Smith of the British Museum published the Chaldean account of creation from Ashurbanipal's tablets; Wellhausen's theory came in 1878 and the JPS Tanakh in 1917.

review.q: In the documentary hypothesis, which source is Genesis 1:1–2:3 usually assigned to?
review.why: The first creation account, with Elohim and its ordered structure, is assigned to the priestly source P; the garden story is assigned to J.

review.q: Which idea is part of Christian tradition but not mainstream Jewish reading of Genesis 3?
choices: The humans were sent out of Eden
The text uses a pun on naked and cunning
Humans inherit a fallen state from Adam
review.why: Original sin is Augustine's doctrine; Jewish tradition reads the chapter as explaining death and exile while each person chooses between two inclinations.

review.q: How many times does Abraham say hineni in Genesis 22, and to whom?
choices: Three times: to God, to Isaac, to the angel
review.why: Abraham answers "here am I" to God in verse 1, to Isaac in verse 7 and to the angel in verse 11.

review.q: Why did Auerbach set Genesis 22 beside a scene from Homer?
choices: To show Genesis leaves nearly everything unspoken while Homer lights everything
review.why: Mimesis opens with this comparison of two styles; the biblical style, Auerbach said, is "fraught with background."

review.q: Which reader concluded that Isaac was a boy near 13, from what the text does not say?
review.why: Ibn Ezra argued that a grown Isaac's willingness would have been recorded as a merit; Genesis Rabbah gives 37, and Ramban discusses the nature of the test.
